Object References and Aliasing in AP CSA

In Java, object variables don’t store the object itself — they store a reference (memory address) to where the object lives on the heap. This distinction causes some of the trickiest AP exam questions.

Primitives vs References

Primitive (int, double, boolean) Reference (Object, String, array)
Stores the actual value Stores a memory address
int x = 5; — x holds 5 Dog d = new Dog(); — d holds address
Copied by value Copied by reference

Aliasing: Two Variables, One Object

When you assign one object variable to another, both variables point to the same object. Changing the object through one variable changes it for the other too.

int[] a = {1, 2, 3};
int[] b = a;       // b is an ALIAS for a -- same array

b[0] = 99;
System.out.println(a[0]);  // 99 -- a was changed too!
⚠ Alias Trap: A very common AP question shows two variables modified and asks what the original contains. If an object was assigned (not copied), both variables see the change.

null References

A reference variable that hasn’t been assigned an object holds null. Calling a method on null causes a NullPointerException at runtime.

String s = null;
System.out.println(s.length());  // NullPointerException!

AP CSA › Unit 4 › Parallel Arrays

Parallel Arrays in AP CSA

Parallel arrays are two or more arrays of the same length where corresponding indices represent related data. Index 0 in array A goes with index 0 in array B, and so on.

Structure

String[] names  = {"Alice", "Bob", "Carol", "Dave"};
int[]    scores = {92, 78, 85, 91};

// names[0] = "Alice" and scores[0] = 92 are related
// names[1] = "Bob"   and scores[1] = 78 are related

Common Operations

// Print all name-score pairs
for (int i = 0; i < names.length; i++) {
    System.out.println(names[i] + ": " + scores[i]);
}

// Find the name with the highest score
int maxIdx = 0;
for (int i = 1; i < scores.length; i++) {
    if (scores[i] > scores[maxIdx]) {
        maxIdx = i;
    }
}
System.out.println("Top scorer: " + names[maxIdx]);
Key Pattern: Track the index of the max/min, not just the value, so you can look up the corresponding element in the other array.

📝 Practice Question 1

Parallel arrays names (String[]) and ages (int[]) each have 5 elements. Which code correctly prints the name of the oldest person?

✅ Exam Tip: Parallel array problems almost always require tracking an index, not a value. When asked to find a name/label associated with a max or min, initialize int maxIdx = 0 and update it — never just track the numeric maximum.

AP CSA › Unit 1 › Pass-by-Value

Pass-by-Value in Java (AP CSA)

Java is always pass-by-value. When you pass an argument to a method, the method gets a copy of that value. Changes to the parameter inside the method do not affect the original variable.

Primitives: Copy of the Value

public static void addTen(int num) {
    num = num + 10;    // changes the LOCAL copy only
    System.out.println("Inside: " + num);
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    int x = 5;
    addTen(x);
    System.out.println("Outside: " + x);  // still 5!
}

Output: Inside: 15 then Outside: 5. The original x is unchanged.

Objects: Copy of the Reference

When you pass an object, Java copies the reference (address). The method gets its own copy of the reference, but both copies point to the same object. So you can change the object’s contents, but you can’t make the original variable point somewhere else.

public static void changeFirst(int[] arr) {
    arr[0] = 999;    // modifies the actual array object
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    int[] nums = {1, 2, 3};
    changeFirst(nums);
    System.out.println(nums[0]);  // 999 -- the object WAS changed
}
⚠ The Tricky Part: You can change what’s inside an object but you cannot change what object the original variable points to. Reassigning the parameter (arr = new int[5]) inside a method has no effect outside.

What is printed by the following code?

public static void doubleIt(int x) {
    x = x * 2;
}
public static void main(String[] args) {
    int val = 7;
    doubleIt(val);
    System.out.println(val);
}

📝 Practice Question 2

Which of the following statements about passing arguments in Java is correct?

I. Primitive arguments are passed by value; the original cannot be changed by the method.
II. When an array is passed, changes to array elements inside the method affect the original array.
III. When an array is passed, reassigning the parameter to a new array inside the method changes the original variable.

✅ Exam Tip: AP exam questions about pass-by-value often show a method that appears to change a variable but doesn’t. The answer is always: if it’s a primitive, the original is unchanged. If it’s an array/object, the elements can be changed but the reference cannot be redirected.

AP CSA › Unit 3 › Writing Classes

Writing Classes in AP CSA

FRQ #2 on every AP CSA exam asks you to write a complete class from scratch. This is one of the most predictable point sources on the exam — master the anatomy of a class and you’re guaranteed partial credit at minimum.

Anatomy of a Class

public class Dog {
    // 1. Private instance variables
    private String name;
    private int age;

    // 2. Constructor
    public Dog(String name, int age) {
        this.name = name;
        this.age = age;
    }

    // 3. Accessor (getter)
    public String getName() {
        return name;
    }

    // 4. Mutator (setter)
    public void setAge(int newAge) {
        age = newAge;
    }

    // 5. Other methods
    public String toString() {
        return name + " is " + age + " years old";
    }
}
The 5 Parts: Instance variables (private), constructor, accessors, mutators, and other methods. The AP rubric awards points for each piece independently — even if one part has a bug, you can still earn points for others.

The this Keyword

When a parameter name matches an instance variable name, use this to distinguish them:

public Dog(String name, int age) {
    this.name = name;  // this.name = instance variable
    this.age = age;    // age alone = parameter
}
